# async_trait - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/async-trait/^0.1/

## Expand description

#### Type erasure for async trait methods

The stabilization of async functions in traits in Rust 1.75 did not include
support for using traits containing async functions as `dyn Trait`. Trying
to use dyn with an async trait produces the following error:

```
error[E0038]: the trait `Trait` is not dyn compatible
 --> src/main.rs:5:22
  |
5 | pub fn make() -> Box<dyn Trait> {
  |                      ^^^^^^^^^ `Trait` is not dyn compatible
  |
note: for a trait to be dyn compatible it needs to allow building a vtable
      for more information, visit <https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility>
 --> src/main.rs:2:14
  |
1 | pub trait Trait {
  |           ----- this trait is not dyn compatible...
2 |     async fn f(&self);
  |              ^ ...because method `f` is `async`
  = help: consider moving `f` to another trait
```
This crate provides an attribute macro to make async fn in traits work with dyn traits.

Please refer to [ why async fn in traits are hard](https://smallcultfollowing.com/babysteps/blog/2019/10/26/async-fn-in-traits-are-hard/) for a deeper
analysis of how this implementation differs from what the compiler and
language deliver natively.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example implements the core of a highly effective advertising platform using async fn in a trait.

The only thing to notice here is that we write an `#[async_trait]` macro on
top of traits and trait impls that contain async fn, and then they work. We
get to have `Vec<Box<dyn Advertisement + Sync>>` or `&[&dyn Advertisement]`,
for example.

```
use async_trait::async_trait;
#[async_trait]
trait Advertisement {
    async fn run(&self);
}
struct Modal;
#[async_trait]
impl Advertisement for Modal {
    async fn run(&self) {
        self.render_fullscreen().await;
        for _ in 0..4u16 {
            remind_user_to_join_mailing_list().await;
        }
        self.hide_for_now().await;
    }
}
struct AutoplayingVideo {
    media_url: String,
}
#[async_trait]
impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo {
    async fn run(&self) {
        let stream = connect(&self.media_url).await;
        stream.play().await;
        // Video probably persuaded user to join our mailing list!
        Modal.run().await;
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-features)Supported features

It is the intention that all features of Rust traits should work nicely with
#[async_trait], but the edge cases are numerous. Please file an issue if
you see unexpected borrow checker errors, type errors, or warnings. There is
no use of `unsafe` in the expanded code, so rest assured that if your code
compiles it can’t be that badly broken.

☑ Self by value, by reference, by mut reference, or no self;

☑ Any number of arguments, any return value;

☑ Generic type parameters and lifetime parameters;

☑ Associated types;

☑ Having async and non-async functions in the same trait;

☑ Default implementations provided by the trait;

☑ Elided lifetimes.

[§](https://docs.rs#explanation)Explanation

Async fns get transformed into methods that return `Pin<Box<dyn Future + Send + 'async_trait>>` and delegate to an async block.

For example the `impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo` above would be
expanded as:

```
impl Advertisement for AutoplayingVideo {
    fn run<'async_trait>(
        &'async_trait self,
    ) -> Pin<Box<dyn core::future::Future<Output = ()> + Send + 'async_trait>>
    where
        Self: Sync + 'async_trait,
    {
        Box::pin(async move {
            /* the original method body */
        })
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-threadsafe-futures)Non-threadsafe futures

Not all async traits need futures that are `dyn Future + Send`. To avoid
having Send and Sync bounds placed on the async trait methods, invoke the
async trait macro as `#[async_trait(?Send)]` on both the trait and the impl
blocks.

[§](https://docs.rs#elided-lifetimes)Elided lifetimes

Be aware that async fn syntax does not allow lifetime elision outside of `&`
and `&mut` references. (This is true even when not using #[async_trait].)
Lifetimes must be named or marked by the placeholder `'_`.

Fortunately the compiler is able to diagnose missing lifetimes with a good error message.

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
type Elided<'a> = &'a usize;
#[async_trait]
trait Test {
    async fn test(not_okay: Elided, okay: &usize) {}
}
```
```
error[E0726]: implicit elided lifetime not allowed here
 --> src/main.rs:9:29
  |
9 |     async fn test(not_okay: Elided, okay: &usize) {}
  |                             ^^^^^^- help: indicate the anonymous lifetime: `<'_>`
```
The fix is to name the lifetime or use `'_`.

```
#[async_trait]
trait Test {
    // either
    async fn test<'e>(elided: Elided<'e>) {}
    // or
    async fn test(elided: Elided<'_>) {}
}
```

---

# chrono - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/chrono/^0.4/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#chrono-date-and-time-for-rust)Chrono: Date and Time for Rust

Chrono aims to provide all functionality needed to do correct operations on dates and times in
the [proleptic Gregorian calendar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proleptic_Gregorian_calendar):

- The `DateTime`
- Operations that may produce an invalid or ambiguous date and time return `Option`or`MappedLocalTime`
- Configurable parsing and formatting with a `strftime`inspired date and time formatting syntax.
- The `Local`
- Types and operations are implemented to be reasonably efficient.

Timezone data is not shipped with chrono by default to limit binary sizes. Use the companion
crate [Chrono-TZ](https://crates.io/crates/chrono-tz) or [ tzfile](https://crates.io/crates/tzfile) for full timezone support.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Chrono supports various runtime environments and operating systems, and has several features that may be enabled or disabled.

Default features:

- `alloc`: Enable features that depend on allocation (primarily string formatting).
- `std`: Enables functionality that depends on the standard library. This is a superset of- `alloc`and adds interoperation with standard library types and traits.
- `clock`: Enables reading the local timezone (- `Local`). This is a superset of- `now`.
- `now`: Enables reading the system time (- `now`).
- `wasmbind`: Interface with the JS Date API for the- `wasm32`target.

Optional features:

- `serde`: Enable serialization/deserialization via- [serde](https://github.com/serde-rs/serde).
- `rkyv`: Deprecated, use the- `rkyv-*`features.
- `rkyv-16`: Enable serialization/deserialization via- [rkyv](https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv), using 16-bit integers for integral- `*size`types.
- `rkyv-32`: Enable serialization/deserialization via- [rkyv](https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv), using 32-bit integers for integral- `*size`types.
- `rkyv-64`: Enable serialization/deserialization via- [rkyv](https://github.com/rkyv/rkyv), using 64-bit integers for integral- `*size`types.
- `rkyv-validation`: Enable rkyv validation support using- `bytecheck`.
- `arbitrary`: Construct arbitrary instances of a type with the Arbitrary crate.
- `unstable-locales`: Enable localization. This adds various methods with a- `_localized`suffix. The implementation and API may change or even be removed in a patch release. Feedback welcome.
- `oldtime`: This feature no longer has any effect; it used to offer compatibility with the- `time`0.1 crate.

Note: The `rkyv{,-16,-32,-64}` features are mutually exclusive.

See the [cargo docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/specifying-dependencies.html#choosing-features) for examples of specifying features.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

[§](https://docs.rs#time-delta--duration)Time delta / Duration

Chrono has a [ TimeDelta](https://docs.rs/struct.TimeDelta.html) type to represent the magnitude of a time span. This is an “accurate”
duration represented as seconds and nanoseconds, and does not represent “nominal” components
such as days or months.

The [ TimeDelta](https://docs.rs/struct.TimeDelta.html) type was previously named

`Duration` (and is still available as a type alias
with that name). A notable difference with the similar [is that it is a signed value instead of unsigned.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)

`core::time::Duration`Chrono currently only supports a small number of operations with [ core::time::Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html).
You can convert between both types with the

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.TimeDelta.html#method.from_std)

`TimeDelta::from_std`[methods.](https://docs.rs/struct.TimeDelta.html#method.to_std)

`TimeDelta::to_std`[§](https://docs.rs#date-and-time)Date and Time

Chrono provides a [ DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html) type to represent a date and a time in a timezone.

For more abstract moment-in-time tracking such as internal timekeeping that is unconcerned with
timezones, consider [ std::time::SystemTime](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/time/struct.SystemTime.html), which tracks your system clock, or

[, which is an opaque but monotonically-increasing representation of a moment in time.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/time/struct.Instant.html)

`std::time::Instant`[ DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html) is timezone-aware and must be constructed from a

[object, which defines how the local date is converted to and back from the UTC date. There are three well-known](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html)

`TimeZone`[implementations:](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html)

`TimeZone`-
`Utc`
-
`Local`
-
`FixedOffset``TimeZone`s into this type.

[ DateTime](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)s with different

[types are distinct and do not mix, but can be converted to each other using the](https://docs.rs/trait.TimeZone.html)

`TimeZone`[method.](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.with_timezone)

`DateTime::with_timezone`You can get the current date and time in the UTC time zone ([ Utc::now()](https://docs.rs/struct.Utc.html#method.now)) or in the local time
zone (

[).](https://docs.rs/struct.Local.html#method.now)

`Local::now()````
use chrono::prelude::*;
let utc: DateTime<Utc> = Utc::now(); // e.g. `2014-11-28T12:45:59.324310806Z`
```
```
use chrono::prelude::*;
let local: DateTime<Local> = Local::now(); // e.g. `2014-11-28T21:45:59.324310806+09:00`
```
Alternatively, you can create your own date and time. This is a bit verbose due to Rust’s lack of function and method overloading, but in turn we get a rich combination of initialization methods.

```
use chrono::offset::MappedLocalTime;
use chrono::prelude::*;
let dt = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11).unwrap(); // `2014-07-08T09:10:11Z`
assert_eq!(
    dt,
    NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
        .and_hms_opt(9, 10, 11)?
        .and_utc()
);
// July 8 is 188th day of the year 2014 (`o` for "ordinal")
assert_eq!(dt, NaiveDate::from_yo_opt(2014, 189)?.and_hms_opt(9, 10, 11)?.and_utc());
// July 8 is Tuesday in ISO week 28 of the year 2014.
assert_eq!(
    dt,
    NaiveDate::from_isoywd_opt(2014, 28, Weekday::Tue)?.and_hms_opt(9, 10, 11)?.and_utc()
);
let dt = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
    .and_hms_milli_opt(9, 10, 11, 12)?
    .and_utc(); // `2014-07-08T09:10:11.012Z`
assert_eq!(
    dt,
    NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
        .and_hms_micro_opt(9, 10, 11, 12_000)?
        .and_utc()
);
assert_eq!(
    dt,
    NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?
        .and_hms_nano_opt(9, 10, 11, 12_000_000)?
        .and_utc()
);
// dynamic verification
assert_eq!(
    Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 8, 21, 15, 33),
    MappedLocalTime::Single(
        NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)?.and_hms_opt(21, 15, 33)?.and_utc()
    )
);
assert_eq!(Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 8, 80, 15, 33), MappedLocalTime::None);
assert_eq!(Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 7, 38, 21, 15, 33), MappedLocalTime::None);
// other time zone objects can be used to construct a local datetime.
// obviously, `local_dt` is normally different from `dt`, but `fixed_dt` should be identical.
let local_dt = Local
    .from_local_datetime(
        &NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8).unwrap().and_hms_milli_opt(9, 10, 11, 12).unwrap(),
    )
    .unwrap();
let fixed_dt = FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600)
    .unwrap()
    .from_local_datetime(
        &NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 7, 8)
            .unwrap()
            .and_hms_milli_opt(18, 10, 11, 12)
            .unwrap(),
    )
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt, fixed_dt);
```
Various properties are available to the date and time, and can be altered individually. Most of
them are defined in the traits [ Datelike](https://docs.rs/trait.Datelike.html) and

[which you should](https://docs.rs/trait.Timelike.html)

`Timelike``use` before.
Addition and subtraction is also supported.
The following illustrates most supported operations to the date and time:```
use chrono::prelude::*;
use chrono::TimeDelta;
// assume this returned `2014-11-28T21:45:59.324310806+09:00`:
let dt = FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600)
    .unwrap()
    .from_local_datetime(
        &NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 11, 28)
            .unwrap()
            .and_hms_nano_opt(21, 45, 59, 324310806)
            .unwrap(),
    )
    .unwrap();
// property accessors
assert_eq!((dt.year(), dt.month(), dt.day()), (2014, 11, 28));
assert_eq!((dt.month0(), dt.day0()), (10, 27)); // for unfortunate souls
assert_eq!((dt.hour(), dt.minute(), dt.second()), (21, 45, 59));
assert_eq!(dt.weekday(), Weekday::Fri);
assert_eq!(dt.weekday().number_from_monday(), 5); // Mon=1, ..., Sun=7
assert_eq!(dt.ordinal(), 332); // the day of year
assert_eq!(dt.num_days_from_ce(), 735565); // the number of days from and including Jan 1, 1
// time zone accessor and manipulation
assert_eq!(dt.offset().fix().local_minus_utc(), 9 * 3600);
assert_eq!(dt.timezone(), FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600).unwrap());
assert_eq!(
    dt.with_timezone(&Utc),
    NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 11, 28)
        .unwrap()
        .and_hms_nano_opt(12, 45, 59, 324310806)
        .unwrap()
        .and_utc()
);
// a sample of property manipulations (validates dynamically)
assert_eq!(dt.with_day(29).unwrap().weekday(), Weekday::Sat); // 2014-11-29 is Saturday
assert_eq!(dt.with_day(32), None);
assert_eq!(dt.with_year(-300).unwrap().num_days_from_ce(), -109606); // November 29, 301 BCE
// arithmetic operations
let dt1 = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 14, 8, 9, 10).unwrap();
let dt2 = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 14, 10, 9, 8).unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt1.signed_duration_since(dt2), TimeDelta::try_seconds(-2 * 3600 + 2).unwrap());
assert_eq!(dt2.signed_duration_since(dt1), TimeDelta::try_seconds(2 * 3600 - 2).unwrap());
assert_eq!(
    Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap()
        + TimeDelta::try_seconds(1_000_000_000).unwrap(),
    Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2001, 9, 9, 1, 46, 40).unwrap()
);
assert_eq!(
    Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(1970, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0).unwrap()
        - TimeDelta::try_seconds(1_000_000_000).unwrap(),
    Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(1938, 4, 24, 22, 13, 20).unwrap()
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-and-parsing)Formatting and Parsing

Formatting is done via the [ format](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.format) method, which format is equivalent to
the familiar

`strftime` format.See [ format::strftime](https://docs.rs/format/strftime/index.html#specifiers) documentation for full syntax and list of
specifiers.

The default `to_string` method and `{:?}` specifier also give a reasonable representation.
Chrono also provides [ to_rfc2822](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.to_rfc2822) and

[methods for well-known formats.](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.to_rfc3339)

`to_rfc3339`Chrono now also provides date formatting in almost any language without the help of an
additional C library. This functionality is under the feature `unstable-locales`:

`chrono = { version = "0.4", features = ["unstable-locales"] }`The `unstable-locales` feature requires and implies at least the `alloc` feature.

```
use chrono::prelude::*;
let dt = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 28, 12, 0, 9).unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.format("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S").to_string(), "2014-11-28 12:00:09");
assert_eq!(dt.format("%a %b %e %T %Y").to_string(), "Fri Nov 28 12:00:09 2014");
assert_eq!(
    dt.format_localized("%A %e %B %Y, %T", Locale::fr_BE).to_string(),
    "vendredi 28 novembre 2014, 12:00:09"
);
assert_eq!(dt.format("%a %b %e %T %Y").to_string(), dt.format("%c").to_string());
assert_eq!(dt.to_string(), "2014-11-28 12:00:09 UTC");
assert_eq!(dt.to_rfc2822(), "Fri, 28 Nov 2014 12:00:09 +0000");
assert_eq!(dt.to_rfc3339(), "2014-11-28T12:00:09+00:00");
assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", dt), "2014-11-28T12:00:09Z");
// Note that milli/nanoseconds are only printed if they are non-zero
let dt_nano = NaiveDate::from_ymd_opt(2014, 11, 28)
    .unwrap()
    .and_hms_nano_opt(12, 0, 9, 1)
    .unwrap()
    .and_utc();
assert_eq!(format!("{:?}", dt_nano), "2014-11-28T12:00:09.000000001Z");
```
Parsing can be done with two methods:

-
The standard `FromStr``parse``DateTime<FixedOffset>`,`DateTime<Utc>`and`DateTime<Local>`values. This parses what the`{:?}`(`std::fmt::Debug`
-
`DateTime::parse_from_str``DateTime<FixedOffset>`. This should be used when the offset is a part of input and the caller cannot guess that. It*cannot*be used when the offset can be missing.`DateTime::parse_from_rfc2822``DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339`

More detailed control over the parsing process is available via [ format](https://docs.rs/format/index.html) module.

```
use chrono::prelude::*;
let dt = Utc.with_ymd_and_hms(2014, 11, 28, 12, 0, 9).unwrap();
let fixed_dt = dt.with_timezone(&FixedOffset::east_opt(9 * 3600).unwrap());
// method 1
assert_eq!("2014-11-28T12:00:09Z".parse::<DateTime<Utc>>(), Ok(dt.clone()));
assert_eq!("2014-11-28T21:00:09+09:00".parse::<DateTime<Utc>>(), Ok(dt.clone()));
assert_eq!("2014-11-28T21:00:09+09:00".parse::<DateTime<FixedOffset>>(), Ok(fixed_dt.clone()));
// method 2
assert_eq!(
    DateTime::parse_from_str("2014-11-28 21:00:09 +09:00", "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S %z"),
    Ok(fixed_dt.clone())
);
assert_eq!(
    DateTime::parse_from_rfc2822("Fri, 28 Nov 2014 21:00:09 +0900"),
    Ok(fixed_dt.clone())
);
assert_eq!(DateTime::parse_from_rfc3339("2014-11-28T21:00:09+09:00"), Ok(fixed_dt.clone()));
// oops, the year is missing!
assert!(DateTime::parse_from_str("Fri Nov 28 12:00:09", "%a %b %e %T %Y").is_err());
// oops, the format string does not include the year at all!
assert!(DateTime::parse_from_str("Fri Nov 28 12:00:09", "%a %b %e %T").is_err());
// oops, the weekday is incorrect!
assert!(DateTime::parse_from_str("Sat Nov 28 12:00:09 2014", "%a %b %e %T %Y").is_err());
```
Again: See [ format::strftime](https://docs.rs/format/strftime/index.html#specifiers) documentation for full syntax and
list of specifiers.

[§](https://docs.rs#conversion-from-and-to-epoch-timestamps)Conversion from and to EPOCH timestamps

Use [ DateTime::from_timestamp(seconds, nanoseconds)](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.from_timestamp)
to construct a

[from a UNIX timestamp (seconds, nanoseconds that passed since January 1st 1970).](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)

`DateTime<Utc>`Use [ DateTime.timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.timestamp) to get the timestamp (in seconds)
from a

[. Additionally, you can use](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html)

`DateTime`[to get the number of additional number of nanoseconds.](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.timestamp_subsec_nanos)

`DateTime.timestamp_subsec_nanos````
// We need the trait in scope to use Utc::timestamp().
use chrono::{DateTime, Utc};
// Construct a datetime from epoch:
let dt: DateTime<Utc> = DateTime::from_timestamp_secs(1_500_000_000).unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.to_rfc2822(), "Fri, 14 Jul 2017 02:40:00 +0000");
// Get epoch value from a datetime:
let dt = DateTime::parse_from_rfc2822("Fri, 14 Jul 2017 02:40:00 +0000").unwrap();
assert_eq!(dt.timestamp(), 1_500_000_000);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#naive-date-and-time)Naive date and time

Chrono provides naive counterparts to `Date`, (non-existent) `Time` and `DateTime` as
[ NaiveDate](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDate.html),

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveTime.html)

`NaiveTime`[respectively.](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveDateTime.html)

`NaiveDateTime`They have almost equivalent interfaces as their timezone-aware twins, but are not associated to time zones obviously and can be quite low-level. They are mostly useful for building blocks for higher-level types.

Timezone-aware `DateTime` and `Date` types have two methods returning naive versions:
[ naive_local](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.naive_local) returns a view to the naive local time,
and

[returns a view to the naive UTC time.](https://docs.rs/struct.DateTime.html#method.naive_utc)

`naive_utc`[§](https://docs.rs#limitations)Limitations

- Only the proleptic Gregorian calendar (i.e. extended to support older dates) is supported.
- Date types are limited to about +/- 262,000 years from the common epoch.
- Time types are limited to nanosecond accuracy.
- Leap seconds can be represented, but Chrono does not fully support them.
See [Leap Second Handling](https://docs.rs/struct.NaiveTime.html#leap-second-handling).

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version-requirements)Rust version requirements

The Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV) is currently **Rust 1.61.0**.

The MSRV is explicitly tested in CI. It may be bumped in minor releases, but this is not done lightly.

[§](https://docs.rs#relation-between-chrono-and-time-01)Relation between chrono and time 0.1

Rust first had a `time` module added to `std` in its 0.7 release. It later moved to
`libextra`, and then to a `libtime` library shipped alongside the standard library. In 2014
work on chrono started in order to provide a full-featured date and time library in Rust.
Some improvements from chrono made it into the standard library; notably, `chrono::Duration`
was included as `std::time::Duration` ([rust#15934](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/15934)) in 2014.

In preparation of Rust 1.0 at the end of 2014 `libtime` was moved out of the Rust distro and
into the `time` crate to eventually be redesigned ([rust#18832](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/18832#issuecomment-62448221), [rust#18858](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/18858)), like the
`num` and `rand` crates. Of course chrono kept its dependency on this `time` crate. `time`
started re-exporting `std::time::Duration` during this period. Later, the standard library was
changed to have a more limited unsigned `Duration` type ([rust#24920](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/24920), [RFC 1040](https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/1040-duration-reform.html)), while the
`time` crate kept the full functionality with `time::Duration`. `time::Duration` had been a
part of chrono’s public API.

By 2016 `time` 0.1 lived under the `rust-lang-deprecated` organisation and was not actively
maintained ([time#136](https://github.com/time-rs/time/issues/136)). chrono absorbed the platform functionality and `Duration` type of the
`time` crate in [chrono#478](https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/478) (the work started in [chrono#286](https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/286)). In order to preserve
compatibility with downstream crates depending on `time` and `chrono` sharing a `Duration`
type, chrono kept depending on time 0.1. chrono offered the option to opt out of the `time`
dependency by disabling the `oldtime` feature (swapping it out for an effectively similar
chrono type). In 2019, @jhpratt took over maintenance on the `time` crate and released what
amounts to a new crate as `time` 0.2.

[§](https://docs.rs#security-advisories)Security advisories

In November of 2020 [CVE-2020-26235](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2020-26235) and [RUSTSEC-2020-0071](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2020-0071) were opened against the `time` crate.
@quininer had found that calls to `localtime_r` may be unsound ([chrono#499](https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/499)). Eventually, almost
a year later, this was also made into a security advisory against chrono as [RUSTSEC-2020-0159](https://rustsec.org/advisories/RUSTSEC-2020-0159.html),
which had platform code similar to `time`.

On Unix-like systems a process is given a timezone id or description via the `TZ` environment
variable. We need this timezone data to calculate the current local time from a value that is
in UTC, such as the time from the system clock. `time` 0.1 and chrono used the POSIX function
`localtime_r` to do the conversion to local time, which reads the `TZ` variable.

Rust assumes the environment to be writable and uses locks to access it from multiple threads.
Some other programming languages and libraries use similar locking strategies, but these are
typically not shared across languages. More importantly, POSIX declares modifying the
environment in a multi-threaded process as unsafe, and `getenv` in libc can’t be changed to
take a lock because it returns a pointer to the data (see [rust#27970](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/27970) for more discussion).

Since version 4.20 chrono no longer uses `localtime_r`, instead using Rust code to query the
timezone (from the `TZ` variable or via `iana-time-zone` as a fallback) and work with data
from the system timezone database directly. The code for this was forked from the [tz-rs crate](https://crates.io/crates/tz-rs)
by @x-hgg-x. As such, chrono now respects the Rust lock when reading the `TZ` environment
variable. In general, code should avoid modifying the environment.

[§](https://docs.rs#removing-time-01)Removing time 0.1

Because time 0.1 has been unmaintained for years, however, the security advisory mentioned
above has not been addressed. While chrono maintainers were careful not to break backwards
compatibility with the `time::Duration` type, there has been a long stream of issues from
users inquiring about the time 0.1 dependency with the vulnerability. We investigated the
potential breakage of removing the time 0.1 dependency in [chrono#1095](https://github.com/chronotope/chrono/pull/1095) using a crater-like
experiment and determined that the potential for breaking (public) dependencies is very low.
We reached out to those few crates that did still depend on compatibility with time 0.1.

As such, for chrono 0.4.30 we have decided to swap out the time 0.1 `Duration` implementation
for a local one that will offer a strict superset of the existing API going forward. This
will prevent most downstream users from being affected by the security vulnerability in time
0.1 while minimizing the ecosystem impact of semver-incompatible version churn.

# ikigai_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ikigai-core/^0.1.32/

## Expand description

`ikigai-core` — the resolution kernel spine.

M0 establishes the identity model that everything else resolves through:

- `Iri`
- `Verb`
- `ArgRef`
- `Request`- `RequestId`
- `Representation`- `ReprType`- `ContentId`
- `Capability`

The identity model is content-addressed: equal inputs collapse to equal identities, so caching and de-duplication fall out by construction.

M1 adds resolution: a [ Request](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html) is matched by a

[within a](https://docs.rs/trait.Grammar.html)

`Grammar`[to an](https://docs.rs/trait.Space.html)

`Space`[that produces a](https://docs.rs/trait.Endpoint.html)

`Endpoint`[. Spaces compose via](https://docs.rs/struct.Representation.html)

`Representation`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Mount.html)

`Mount`[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Fallback.html)

`Fallback`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.Rewrite.html)

`Rewrite`[§](https://docs.rs#naming-conventions)Naming conventions

Two namespaces, two conventions:

- **Resource identifiers**— IRIs and endpoint names, e.g.- `toUpper`in- `urn:fn:toUpper`— use RDF-idiomatic casing:- `lowerCamelCase`for properties and operations,- `PascalCase`for classes.
- **Rust identifiers**use- `snake_case`and- `PascalCase`per Rust convention.

A `snake_case` constructor therefore maps to a `lowerCamelCase` identifier —
e.g. [ builtins::to_upper](https://docs.rs/builtins/fn.to_upper.html) builds the

`toUpper` endpoint.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [builtins](https://docs.rs/builtins/index.html)
- Small closure-backed endpoints — the simplest, idempotent, perfectly cacheable kind. They double as the M1 demonstration of resolution and the pure-cache test: the same call with the same value has the same identity.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Action](https://docs.rs/struct.ActionMatch.html)- Match
- An endpoint whose required inputs are all satisfiable by a set of available RDF classes — an action you could take given the typed entities present in a context (a layer/canvas).
- [ArgSpec](https://docs.rs/struct.ArgSpec.html)
- A specification of one named input an endpoint accepts.
- [Bindings](https://docs.rs/struct.Bindings.html)
- Variables captured when a grammar matches an identifier.
- [Capability](https://docs.rs/struct.Capability.html)
- An unforgeable handle conferring authority to resolve and invoke resources.
- [Content](https://docs.rs/struct.ContentId.html)- Id
- A content address: a BLAKE3 digest of canonical bytes, rendered as `b3:<hex>`.
- [Content](https://docs.rs/struct.ContentIdError.html)- IdError
- Error parsing a `ContentId`
- [Description](https://docs.rs/struct.Description.html)
- A structured, RDF-agnostic self-description of an endpoint.
- [Endpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.EndpointSpace.html)- Space
- A leaf space: an ordered set of `(grammar, endpoint)`bindings. The first grammar that matches the request’s target wins.
- [Exact](https://docs.rs/struct.Exact.html)
- Matches one exact identifier and captures no variables.
- [Fallback](https://docs.rs/struct.Fallback.html)
- Try each space in order; the first hit wins.
- [FnEndpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.FnEndpoint.html)
- An endpoint backed by a Rust closure — the simplest, idempotent kind.
- [Invocation](https://docs.rs/struct.Invocation.html)
- The context handed to an endpoint when it is invoked.
- [Iri](https://docs.rs/struct.Iri.html)
- A validated, absolute RDF [IRI](https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf11-concepts/#dfn-iri).
- [IriError](https://docs.rs/struct.IriError.html)
- Error returned when a string is not a valid absolute IRI.
- [Kernel](https://docs.rs/struct.Kernel.html)
- Resolves requests against a root space, invokes the resolved endpoint, and caches cacheable representations by their content-addressed request id.
- [Mount](https://docs.rs/struct.Mount.html)
- Mount a space behind an IRI prefix; only requests whose target starts with the prefix are delegated to the inner space.
- [Provenance](https://docs.rs/struct.Provenance.html)
- The cache **provenance**an upstream pipe stage hands to the next: the expiry and golden threads of whatever produced this request’s*input*.
- [Repr](https://docs.rs/struct.ReprType.html)- Type
- A representation type: a media type plus canonicalized parameters.
- [Representation](https://docs.rs/struct.Representation.html)
- A typed value produced by an endpoint.
- [Request](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html)
- A request: a verb applied to a target resource, with named arguments.
- [Request](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestId.html)- Id
- The content-addressed identity of a `Request`
- [Resolved](https://docs.rs/struct.Resolved.html)
- A successful resolution: the endpoint to invoke and its bindings.
- [Rewrite](https://docs.rs/struct.Rewrite.html)
- Rewrite a request’s target IRI before delegating to an inner space. The rule
returns `Some(new_target)`to rewrite, or`None`to pass the request through unchanged.
- [Scope](https://docs.rs/struct.Scope.html)
- The set of address spaces visible to a request during resolution.
- [Space](https://docs.rs/struct.SpaceEntry.html)- Entry
- One binding in a space, for enumeration: the grammar’s pattern and the name of the endpoint it resolves to.
- [System](https://docs.rs/struct.SystemClock.html)- Clock
- A `Clock``Date.now()`-backed clock;`ikigai-core`itself stays runtime-agnostic.)
- [Template](https://docs.rs/struct.TemplateError.html)- Error
- Error parsing a `UriTemplate`
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/struct.Thread.html)
- A **golden thread**: a named validity token a cached representation can depend on.
- [Time](https://docs.rs/struct.Time.html)
- An absolute instant, milliseconds since the Unix epoch.
- [Trace](https://docs.rs/struct.TraceEvent.html)- Event
- One resolved invocation, as the kernel reports it to an installed `Tracer``trace`command turns a stream of these (from one real resolution) into the execution tree — which**worker thread**each node ran on, how long it took, and whether the cache served it.
- [Transreption](https://docs.rs/struct.Transreption.html)
- The media-type conversions a transreptor supports: it can accept any of `from`and produce any of`to`. Used both to type the endpoint in RDF (`ik:transreptsFrom`/`To`) and to select a transreptor for a needed`from → to`conversion.
- [Transreption](https://docs.rs/struct.TransreptionStep.html)- Step
- One step of a transreption plan: invoke the transreptor at `endpoint`with the input piped as`content`and`as`set to`to`.
- [UriTemplate](https://docs.rs/struct.UriTemplate.html)
- A constrained RFC 6570 URI template — Level 1 `{var}`expansion only.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [ArgRef](https://docs.rs/enum.ArgRef.html)
- How an argument value is supplied to a request.
- [Endpoint](https://docs.rs/enum.EndpointKind.html)- Kind
- What *kind*of endpoint this is — a first-class type that projects to an RDF class (`ik:Endpoint`,`ik:Transreptor`, …) and lets the kernel select endpoints by role.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Errors raised during resolution and endpoint invocation.
- [Expiry](https://docs.rs/enum.Expiry.html)
- How long a representation stays valid in the cache.
- [Input](https://docs.rs/enum.InputSource.html)- Source
- Where an input’s value comes from — the two channels an endpoint can read a parameter through.
- [Resolution](https://docs.rs/enum.Resolution.html)
- The outcome of resolving a request against a space.
- [Verb](https://docs.rs/enum.Verb.html)
- The request verbs.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CANONICAL](https://docs.rs/constant.CANONICAL.html)
- The canonical RDF media type the transreptor graph hubs on — the pivot for two-hop conversions when no direct transreptor exists.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Clock](https://docs.rs/trait.Clock.html)
- The kernel’s source of “now”. Injected (rather than read from the system
directly) so pure resolution stays deterministic and replayable: a test or a
replay harness supplies a fixed or recorded clock. Only entries with a
time-based `Expiry::At`
- [Endpoint](https://docs.rs/trait.Endpoint.html)
- An endpoint produces a `Representation`
- [Grammar](https://docs.rs/trait.Grammar.html)
- A grammar decides whether an identifier belongs to an endpoint and, if so, extracts variable bindings from it. Resolution matches a request’s target against the grammars in scope.
- [Issuer](https://docs.rs/trait.Issuer.html)
- Lets an endpoint issue sub-requests back through the kernel. Implemented by
the `Kernel``Invocation``source`/`issue`are unavailable when testing an endpoint in isolation.
- [Meta](https://docs.rs/trait.MetaRenderer.html)- Renderer
- Renders an endpoint’s self-description into a target representation type
(e.g. `text/turtle`,`text/plain`,`text/html`).
- [Scheduler](https://docs.rs/trait.SchedulerReporter.html)- Reporter
- A read-only view of the host scheduler’s live state, injected into the kernel
like a `Clock``urn:kernel:scheduler`can report it**intrinsically**— over the wire and without the host binding an endpoint, uniform with`urn:kernel:cache`and`urn:kernel:threads`. The kernel never*drives*the scheduler (which lives above it, runtime-free); it only reads these rows. With none injected,`urn:kernel:scheduler`reports the single-threaded default.
- [Space](https://docs.rs/trait.Space.html)
- A space maps requests to endpoints by resolution. Spaces compose via the
`Mount``Fallback``Rewrite`
- [Spawner](https://docs.rs/trait.Spawner.html)
- Runs futures concurrently on the host’s executor. Injected into the kernel like
`Clock``Kernel::into_scheduled``ikigai-scheduler`implements it. With no spawner,`Invocation::fan_out`
- [Tracer](https://docs.rs/trait.Tracer.html)
- Receives a `TraceEvent``Kernel::set_tracer``trace`command can capture one real resolution and render it. The host supplies the collector (e.g. a`Mutex<Vec<TraceEvent>>`).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [is_](https://docs.rs/fn.is_auto_invocable.html)- auto_ - invocable
- Whether a transreptor can be invoked automatically — driven with only a piped `content`and a target`as`. True iff every*required*input is`content`or`as`. A transreptor with another required input (e.g.`urn:xslt:transform`’s`stylesheet`) is parameterized and must be invoked explicitly, so it is not auto-selected.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/fn.select_action.html)- action
- Find endpoints in `root`whose required inputs are*fully typed and satisfiable*by`present`— the RDF classes available in a context. An endpoint matches iff it has at least one required input and**every**required input declares an`ArgSpec::class``present`. This is`select_transreptor`**not**applied here.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/fn.select_action_in.html)- action_ - in
- Convenience: select actions over an `Arc<dyn Space>`root (as a kernel holds).
- [select_](https://docs.rs/fn.select_transreptor.html)- transreptor
- Find a chain of auto-invocable transreptors in `root`converting`from`→`to`: a direct single hop if one exists, else a two-hop pivot via`CANONICAL``None`if no chain is available (or if`from == to`, which needs no transreption).
- [select_](https://docs.rs/fn.select_transreptor_in.html)- transreptor_ - in
- Convenience: select over an `Arc<dyn Space>`root (as a kernel holds).

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

# ikigai_org - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/ikigai-org/0.1.0/target-redirect/ikigai_org/

## Expand description

`ikigai-org` — the org-mode agenda as ROC resources.

`urn:org:agenda:{period}` reads **date-fixed events** (headlines with active
`<…>` timestamps, repeaters expanded into the window) from org files and
serves them as text or as the **same skolemized Turtle event graph**
`urn:personal:calendar` speaks — so org and native calendars union and diff
as graphs (the Brian-Busy materialized-view plan).

The org files are read **through the kernel**: the host binds them (e.g. an
`ikigai-fs` space jailed to the org directory at `urn:orgfile:{path}`) and
hands this space their IRIs. That keeps this crate free of filesystem
access — capability-gated, wasm-clean, and golden-thread-ready when the
host’s file space is cacheable.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-parsed-v1)What is parsed (v1)

Headlines (`* Title`) whose section carries an active timestamp:
`<YYYY-MM-DD [Day] [HH:MM[-HH:MM]] [+N{d,w,m,y}]>`. Inactive `[…]`
timestamps are ignored. Untimed stamps are all-day; a timed stamp without
an end defaults to one hour. Repeaters (`+1w`, `+1y`, …) are expanded into
the requested window.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Agenda](https://docs.rs/struct.AgendaEndpoint.html)- Endpoint
- `urn:org:agenda[:{period}]`— the org agenda for a period (default- `week`), sourced through the kernel from the configured org-file resources.
- [OrgEvent](https://docs.rs/struct.OrgEvent.html)
- One agenda event, normalized. The same shape the calendar side speaks.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [agenda_](https://docs.rs/fn.agenda_events.html)- events
- Parse org text into the events overlapping `[win_start, win_end)`, expanding repeaters into the window.
- [space](https://docs.rs/fn.space.html)
- Mount the agenda: `urn:org:agenda`and`urn:org:agenda:{period}`, reading the given org-file resources through the kernel.

---

[46](#46)fn period_range(period: &str, today: NaiveDate) -> Result<(NaiveDate, NaiveDate, String)> {
[49](#49)    let day = |d: NaiveDate| (d, d + Duration::days(1), format!("{d}"));
[50](#50)    let months = [
[51](#51)        "january",
[52](#52)        "february",
[53](#53)        "march",
[54](#54)        "april",
[55](#55)        "may",
[56](#56)        "june",

[58](#58)        "august",
[59](#59)        "september",
[60](#60)        "october",
[61](#61)        "november",
[62](#62)        "december",
[63](#63)    ];
[64](#64)    let range = match period {
[65](#65)        "today" => day(today),
[66](#66)        "tomorrow" => day(today + Duration::days(1)),
[67](#67)        "week" => {
[68](#68)            let monday = today - Duration::days(today.weekday().num_days_from_monday() as i64);
[69](#69)            (
[70](#70)                monday,
[71](#71)                monday + Duration::days(7),
[72](#72)                format!("week of {monday}"),
[73](#73)            )
[74](#74)        }
[75](#75)        "month" => month_range(today.year(), today.month()),
[76](#76)        name if months.contains(&name) => {
[77](#77)            let month = months.iter().position(|m| *m == name).expect("matched") as u32 + 1;
[78](#78)            month_range(today.year(), month)
[79](#79)        }
[80](#80)        other => {
[81](#81)            if let Ok(date) = other.parse::<NaiveDate>() {
[82](#82)                day(date)
[83](#83)            } else if let Some((y, m)) = other
[84](#84)                .split_once('-')
[85](#85)                .and_then(|(y, m)| Some((y.parse::<i32>().ok()?, m.parse::<u32>().ok()?)))
[86](#86)            {
[87](#87)                if !(1..=12).contains(&m) {
[88](#88)                    return Err(bad_period(other));
[89](#89)                }
[90](#90)                month_range(y, m)
[91](#91)            } else {
[92](#92)                return Err(bad_period(other));
[93](#93)            }
[94](#94)        }
[95](#95)    };
[96](#96)    Ok(range)

[129](#129)fn parse_stamp(inner: &str) -> Option<Stamp> {
[131](#131)    let mut date = None;
[132](#132)    let mut time = None;
[133](#133)    let mut repeat = None;
[134](#134)    for part in inner.split_whitespace() {
[135](#135)        if date.is_none() {
[136](#136)            if let Ok(d) = part.parse::<NaiveDate>() {
[137](#137)                date = Some(d);
[138](#138)                continue;
[139](#139)            }
[140](#140)            return None; }
[142](#142)        if let Some(rest) = part.strip_prefix('+') {
[143](#143)            let rest = rest.trim_start_matches('+').trim_start_matches('.');
[146](#146)            if let (Some(unit), Ok(n)) = (
[147](#147)                rest.chars().last().filter(|c| "dwmy".contains(*c)),
[148](#148)                rest[..rest.len().saturating_sub(1)].parse::<u32>(),
[149](#149)            ) {
[150](#150)                repeat = Some((n.max(1), unit));
[151](#151)            }
[152](#152)            continue;
[153](#153)        }
[154](#154)        if part.contains(':') {
[155](#155)            let (from, to) = match part.split_once('-') {
[157](#157)                Some((a, b)) => (a, Some(b)),
[158](#158)                None => (part, None),
[159](#159)            };
[160](#160)            let parse_t = |t: &str| NaiveTime::parse_from_str(t, "%H:%M").ok();
[161](#161)            if let Some(start) = parse_t(from) {
[162](#162)                time = Some((start, to.and_then(parse_t)));
[163](#163)            }
[164](#164)            continue;
[165](#165)        }
[166](#166)        }
[168](#168)    date.map(|date| Stamp {
[169](#169)        date,
[170](#170)        time,
[171](#171)        repeat,
[172](#172)        raw: inner.trim().to_string(),
[173](#173)    })
[174](#174)}

[188](#188)    }

[240](#240)    win_start: NaiveDate,
[241](#241)    win_end: NaiveDate,
[242](#242)) -> Vec<OrgEvent> {
[243](#243)    let mut events = Vec::new();
[244](#244)    let mut headline: Option<String> = None;
[245](#245)    let mut org_id: Option<String> = None;
[246](#246)    for line in org.lines() {
[247](#247)        let trimmed = line.trim_start();
[248](#248)        if let Some(rest) = trimmed
[249](#249)            .strip_prefix('*')
[250](#250)            .filter(|_| trimmed.starts_with('*'))
[251](#251)        {
[252](#252)            let rest = rest.trim_start_matches('*');
[254](#254)            if let Some(title) = rest.strip_prefix(' ') {
[255](#255)                headline = Some(title.trim().to_string());
[256](#256)                org_id = None;
[257](#257)                continue;
[258](#258)            }
[259](#259)        }
[260](#260)        if trimmed.starts_with("# ") || trimmed.starts_with("#+") {
[261](#261)            continue; }
[263](#263)        if let Some(id) = trimmed.strip_prefix(":ID:") {
[264](#264)            org_id = Some(id.trim().to_string());
[265](#265)            continue;
[266](#266)        }
[267](#267)        let Some(title) = &headline else { continue };
[268](#268)        for stamp in stamps_in(line) {
[269](#269)            let base_uid = org_id.clone().unwrap_or_else(|| {
[270](#270)                format!("org-{:016x}", fnv1a(&format!("{title}|{}", stamp.raw)))
[271](#271)            });
[272](#272)            let mut date = stamp.date;
[274](#274)            let mut hops = 0u32;
[275](#275)            while date < win_end && hops < 1000 {
[276](#276)                if date >= win_start {
[277](#277)                    let (start, end, all_day) = match stamp.time {
[278](#278)                        Some((from, to)) => {
[279](#279)                            let until = to.unwrap_or_else(|| {
[280](#280)                                (NaiveDateTime::new(date, from) + Duration::hours(1)).time()
[281](#281)                            });
[282](#282)                            (rfc3339(date, from), rfc3339(date, until), false)
[283](#283)                        }
[284](#284)                        None => {
[285](#285)                            let midnight = NaiveTime::from_hms_opt(0, 0, 0).expect("midnight");
[286](#286)                            (
[287](#287)                                rfc3339(date, midnight),
[288](#288)                                rfc3339(date + Duration::days(1), midnight),
[289](#289)                                true,
[290](#290)                            )
[291](#291)                        }
[292](#292)                    };
[293](#293)                    let uid = if stamp.repeat.is_some() {
[294](#294)                        format!("{base_uid}-{date}")
[295](#295)                    } else {
[296](#296)                        base_uid.clone()
[297](#297)                    };
[298](#298)                    events.push(OrgEvent {
[299](#299)                        uid,
[300](#300)                        title: title.clone(),
[301](#301)                        source: source.to_string(),
[302](#302)                        start,
[303](#303)                        end,
[304](#304)                        all_day,
[305](#305)                    });
[306](#306)                }
[307](#307)                let Some(repeat) = stamp.repeat else { break };
[308](#308)                date = step(date, repeat);
[309](#309)                hops += 1;
[310](#310)            }
[311](#311)        }
[312](#312)    }
[313](#313)    events.sort_by(|a, b| a.start.cmp(&b.start));
[314](#314)    events
[315](#315)}
[316](#316)
[317](#317)fn format_detail(label: &str, events: &[OrgEvent]) -> String {
[320](#320)    if events.is_empty() {
[321](#321)        return format!("org agenda — {label}\n\n  (no events)\n");
[322](#322)    }
[323](#323)    let mut out = format!("org agenda — {label}\n\n");
[324](#324)    for e in events {
[325](#325)        let date = e.start.split_once('T').map(|(d, _)| d).unwrap_or(&e.start);
[326](#326)        let when = if e.all_day {
[327](#327)            format!("{date}  all-day    ")
[328](#328)        } else {
[329](#329)            let hhmm = |s: &str| {
[330](#330)                s.split_once('T')
[331](#331)                    .map(|(_, t)| t[..5.min(t.len())].to_string())
[332](#332)                    .unwrap_or_default()
[333](#333)            };
[334](#334)            format!("{date}  {}-{}", hhmm(&e.start), hhmm(&e.end))
[335](#335)        };
[336](#336)        out.push_str(&format!("  {when}  {}  [{}]\n", e.title, e.source));
[337](#337)    }
[338](#338)    out
[339](#339)}
[340](#340)
[341](#341)fn format_turtle(events: &[OrgEvent]) -> String {
[344](#344)    let mut ttl = String::from(
[345](#345)        "@prefix ical: <http://www.w3.org/2002/12/cal/ical#> .\n\
[346](#346)         @prefix ik: <https://ikigai-rs.dev/ns#> .\n",
[347](#347)    );
[348](#348)    for e in events {
[349](#349)        let mut props = vec![
[350](#350)            "a ical:Vevent".to_string(),
[351](#351)            format!("ical:uid {}", ttl_str(&e.uid)),
[352](#352)            format!("ical:summary {}", ttl_str(&e.title)),
[353](#353)            format!("ical:dtstart {}", ttl_str(&e.start)),
[354](#354)            format!("ical:dtend {}", ttl_str(&e.end)),
[355](#355)            format!("ik:calendar {}", ttl_str(&e.source)),
[356](#356)        ];
[357](#357)        if e.all_day {
[358](#358)            props.push("ik:allDay true".to_string());
[359](#359)        }
[360](#360)        ttl.push_str(&format!(
[361](#361)            "\n<urn:event:{}> {} .\n",
[362](#362)            e.uid.replace(['<', '>', ' '], "-"),
[363](#363)            props.join(" ;\n    ")
[364](#364)        ));
[365](#365)    }
[366](#366)    ttl
[367](#367)}
[368](#368)
[369](#369)fn ttl_str(s: &str) -> String {
[370](#370)    format!(
[371](#371)        "\"{}\"",
[372](#372)        s.replace('\\', "\\\\")
[373](#373)            .replace('"', "\\\"")
[374](#374)            .replace('\n', " ")
[375](#375)    )
[376](#376)}
[377](#377)
[378](#378)pub struct AgendaEndpoint {
[383](#383)    files: Vec<String>,
[385](#385)}
[386](#386)
[387](#387)#[async_trait::async_trait]
[388](#388)impl Endpoint for AgendaEndpoint {
[389](#389)    async fn invoke(&self, inv: &Invocation<'_>) -> Result<Representation> {
[390](#390)        if self.files.is_empty() {
[391](#391)            return Err(Error::Endpoint(
[392](#392)                "urn:org:agenda: no org files configured — add org_dir + org_files to \
[393](#393)                 ~/.config/ikigai/calendar.json"
[394](#394)                    .to_string(),
[395](#395)            ));
[396](#396)        }
[397](#397)        let period = inv
[398](#398)            .bindings
[399](#399)            .get("period")
[400](#400)            .map(str::to_string)
[401](#401)            .unwrap_or_else(|| "week".to_string());
[402](#402)        let (win_start, win_end, label) = period_range(&period, Local::now().date_naive())?;
[403](#403)
[404](#404)        let mut events = Vec::new();
[405](#405)        for file in &self.files {
[406](#406)            let iri = Iri::parse(file.as_str()).map_err(|e| {
[407](#407)                Error::Endpoint(format!("urn:org:agenda: bad file IRI {file}: {e}"))
[408](#408)            })?;
[409](#409)            let repr = inv.source(&iri).await?;
[412](#412)            let text = String::from_utf8(repr.bytes)
[413](#413)                .map_err(|_| Error::Endpoint(format!("urn:org:agenda: {file} is not UTF-8")))?;
[414](#414)            let short = file.rsplit([':', '/']).next().unwrap_or(file).to_string();
[415](#415)            events.extend(agenda_events(&text, &short, win_start, win_end));
[416](#416)        }
[417](#417)        events.sort_by(|a, b| a.start.cmp(&b.start));
[418](#418)
[419](#419)        let want_turtle = inv
[420](#420)            .inline_str("as")
[421](#421)            .map(|s| s.contains("turtle"))
[422](#422)            .unwrap_or(false);
[423](#423)        if want_turtle {
[424](#424)            return Ok(Representation::new(
[425](#425)                ReprType::new("text/turtle").with_param("charset", "utf-8"),
[426](#426)                format_turtle(&events).into_bytes(),
[427](#427)            ));
[428](#428)        }
[429](#429)        Ok(Representation::new(
[430](#430)            ReprType::new("text/plain").with_param("charset", "utf-8"),
[431](#431)            format_detail(&label, &events).into_bytes(),
[432](#432)        ))
[433](#433)    }
[434](#434)
[435](#435)    fn name(&self) -> &str {
[436](#436)        "org-agenda"
[437](#437)    }
[438](#438)
[439](#439)    fn describe(&self) -> Description {
[440](#440)        Description::new("org-agenda")
[441](#441)            .title("Org agenda")
[442](#442)            .summary(
[443](#443)                "Date-fixed events from the configured org files for a period \
[444](#444)                 (urn:org:agenda:{period}: today, tomorrow, week, month, a month name, \
[445](#445)                 YYYY-MM, YYYY-MM-DD; bare = week), repeaters expanded. as=text/turtle \
[446](#446)                 renders the same skolemized event graph as urn:personal:calendar.",
[447](#447)            )
[448](#448)            .verb(Verb::Source)
[449](#449)            .verb(Verb::Meta)
[450](#450)            .input(
[451](#451)                ArgSpec::new("period")
[452](#452)                    .summary("the time window, captured from the IRI (default: week)")
[453](#453)                    .binding(),
[454](#454)            )
[455](#455)            .input(
[456](#456)                ArgSpec::new("as")
[457](#457)                    .summary("text/turtle for the skolemized event graph")
[458](#458)                    .optional(),
[459](#459)            )
[460](#460)            .output("text/plain;charset=utf-8")
[461](#461)    }
[462](#462)}

[464](#464)pub fn space(files: Vec<String>) -> EndpointSpace {
[467](#467)    EndpointSpace::new()
[468](#468)        .bind(
[469](#469)            Exact::new("urn:org:agenda"),
[470](#470)            AgendaEndpoint {
[471](#471)                files: files.clone(),
[472](#472)            },
[473](#473)        )
[474](#474)        .bind(
[475](#475)            UriTemplate::parse("urn:org:agenda:{period}").expect("valid template"),
[476](#476)            AgendaEndpoint { files },
[477](#477)        )

# OrgEvent in ikigai_org - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ikigai-org/0.1.0/ikigai_org/struct.OrgEvent.html

```
pub struct OrgEvent {
    pub uid:
```
[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html),
    pub title: [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html),
    pub source: [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html),
    pub start: [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html),
    pub end: [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html),
    pub all_day: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
}## Expand description

One agenda event, normalized. The same shape the calendar side speaks.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.uid)

`uid: `[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)Stable id: fnv1a of `title|raw-timestamp` (plus the occurrence date for
repeater expansions) — deterministic across runs while the entry is
unedited. An explicit org `:ID:` property, when present, wins.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.title)

`title: `[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)The headline text.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.source)

`source: `[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)The source file’s short name (provenance), e.g. `calendar.org`.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.start)

`start: `[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)Start/end as RFC 3339 local timestamps.
